indicators.label: A/D Line
indicators.theory: The advance/decline line is the best-known breadth indicator and the simplest to compute: each day, take the number of stocks that rose, subtract the number that fell, and add the result to the previous day's value. Every stock counts the same, whatever its size.
indicators.interpretation: Because it isn't cap-weighted, the A/D line shows whether a move is broad or carried by a few giants. Watch for divergences: if the index makes new highs while the A/D line falls, most stocks are no longer participating and the advance is fragile. It is a warning, not a timing signal: divergences can last for months.

indicators.label: ADn Line
indicators.theory: The normalized A/D line, based on the work of Tushar Chande as adapted by Greg Morris: a 21-day stochastic of the advance/decline line (where today's A/D line sits within its range of the last 21 days, 0–100), smoothed with a 7-day exponential average. It works as a short/medium-term breadth dashboard with key levels at 20, 50 and 80.
indicators.interpretation: In the oversold zone (below 20), crossing back above 20 suggests the market is likely to rise in the short term. In the overbought zone (above 80), dropping back below 80 makes a short-term correction likely, and the odds rise if it also crosses 50 downward. An up-impulse is confirmed when it stays above 80 for at least three days; a down-impulse when it closes below 20 even one day. In healthy uptrends it can stay overbought for weeks.

indicators.label: Summation Index & RASI
indicators.theory: The McClellan Summation Index is the running total of the McClellan Oscillator. The ratio-adjusted version (RASI) uses the ratio-adjusted oscillator, so it doesn't depend on how many stocks are counted. Both turn short-term breadth swings into a medium-term trend.
indicators.interpretation: Rising = breadth is improving, falling = deteriorating; the direction matters more than the level. On RASI, +500 is the bullish threshold and −500 the bearish one: a move above +500 is a long-term buy signal, and a fall below −500 shows broad, sustained weakness. Readings beyond ±1,000 are extreme (overbought / oversold). On the standard Summation Index, a new uptrend is usually considered to start with a thrust from −1,000 to at least +2,000.

indicators.label: McClellan Oscillator
indicators.theory: The difference between a 19-day and a 39-day exponential average (10% and 5% smoothing) of ratio-adjusted net advances. It measures the short-term momentum of breadth, much like MACD does for prices.
indicators.interpretation: Above zero, buyers dominate in the short term; below zero, sellers do. Trading the zero crossings alone gives many false signals; extreme overbought or oversold readings are more useful, as they show a high chance of a turn in the next sessions. A swing from below −50 to above +50 is a breadth thrust. Divergences (the index falling to new lows while the oscillator rises) help spot short-term bottoms, especially combined with an ADn line leaving oversold.

indicators.label: New Highs & Lows
indicators.theory: The number of stocks making a new 52-week (one-year) high (green) and a new 52-week low (red) each day, based on intraday highs and lows. Both are drawn from zero on top of each other, so the larger of the two stands out.
indicators.interpretation: New highs outnumbering new lows shows strength; the opposite shows clear weakness and danger. Watch for divergences: new lows rising while the index keeps climbing, or new highs falling while it rises, are warnings (time to tighten stops or hedge). New lows falling after a correction is a good sign. Many investors act when new lows exceed a set share of the market.

indicators.label: % Above Moving Averages
indicators.theory: The percentage of stocks closing above their own 20-day (short term), 50-day (medium term) and 200-day (long term) moving averages. The more stocks take part in a move, the more credible it is. Click a line in the legend to show or hide it.
indicators.interpretation: A market is considered strong with at least 60% of stocks above their 50-day average and weak below 40%. Below 10% is extreme oversold (“blood in the streets”), historically a good time to add exposure. A jump of more than 75 points in under 50 sessions is a first-class breadth thrust that has usually led to gains in the following months (2009, 2011, 2016, 2019, 2020). Divergences against the index are warnings, but can last for weeks.

indicators.label: % Within 5% of Highs & Lows
indicators.theory: The percentage of stocks closing within 5% of their 52-week high (green) and within 5% of their 52-week low (red). If the market is healthy, many stocks will be at or near their highs; if not, something is wrong underneath.
indicators.interpretation: Above 30% of stocks near their highs gives some reassurance about the market; above 40% the market is in a very positive phase. These levels come from all-stock NYSE/Nasdaq data; for the S&P 500 the levels are higher (one study puts the average near 45% when the index returns to highs after a correction). Watch the shape too: the index making higher highs while this line makes lower highs is a lack of strength, stronger if it falls below 30%. More stocks near lows while the market rises is also a danger sign.

indicators.label: Volume Ratios
indicators.theory: Up volume (shares traded in rising stocks) divided by down volume (shares traded in falling stocks), in blue, and its inverse, down ÷ up volume, in orange. A reading of 2 means twice as much volume went into one side as into the other.
indicators.interpretation: Readings above 9 or 10 are rare. A blue spike like that, especially after a fall of 10% or more, marks a day when buyers took control and often starts a medium-term uptrend; several in a few weeks reinforce each other (spring 2009). An orange spike after a fall can be capitulation, with the market exhausted and ready to rebound, ideally confirmed by a strong blue day soon after; at market highs it can warn of exhaustion.
